channel.title: The Librarian's Notebook
channel.description: A commonplace book kept by Mr. Librarian: notes on science and technology, on the world and its news, on the arts, and on whatever else didn't belong in the Ledger, the Regimen or the road. Explainers over hot takes; the working shown; one reader's opinions, labelled as such.

item.title: It Took Its Inventor a Month. The Record Is Now 2.76 Seconds.
item.description: Ernő Rubik built the first Rubik's Cube in 1974 to work out a problem in how solid objects can move, and then needed about a month to solve it himself. The official record now belongs to a nine-year-old in Poland at 2.76 seconds. Here is how a Hungarian classroom model became a 1980s craze, and why the times fell so far once the kids came back to it.

item.title: The Rundown — September 24, 2026

item.title: A Comet Carrying Someone Else's Recipe for Water
item.description: A paper led by Kenji Furuya of Japan's RIKEN institute finds that the water boiling off our solar system's third interstellar visitor, 3I/ATLAS, carries a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio tens of times higher than any comet native to our own solar system — a chemical fingerprint the authors say points to a colder, more metal-poor stellar nursery than the one that built the Sun.

item.title: The Cheapest Fuel in the Solar System Is a Planet
item.description: On September 28, the European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft swings within 8,640 kilometres of Earth over the Indian Ocean, borrowing 3.5 kilometres a second of speed from our planet for free. It's the third of four such thefts on a roundabout route to Jupiter's icy moons that won't actually arrive until 2031 — because JUICE can't carry enough fuel to get there any faster.

item.title: The Chip China Banned Itself Into Building
item.description: On September 22, Alibaba's chip unit T-Head unveiled the Zhenwu V900 at the company's Apsara Conference in Hangzhou — 216GB of on-package memory, a 1,200GB/s interconnect, and clusters scaling to 500,000 units, which CEO Eddie Wu called "the most powerful AI chip in China today." The obvious story is the timing, one day before Xi Jinping landed in Washington for his first US state visit in three years. The more interesting story is who actually kept Nvidia's H200 out of China — and it wasn't only Washington.

item.title: The Chip Doesn't Have to Cross a Border
item.description: On September 18, House Select Committee on China chairman John Moolenaar wrote to Trump urging him to close the "cloud services loophole" in chip export controls. Less than a week before Xi Jinping's first state visit to the White House since 2015, the letter's real weight falls on a second ask: curbing sales of the equipment that makes the chips in the first place.

item.title: Plugin4Shell: A Pin Is Not a Verification
item.description: AIR Security disclosed "Plugin4Shell" on September 17, 2026 — a zero-click flaw in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot and Gemini CLI that let a hijacked git branch silently swap in different code than the one a plugin manifest had pinned by commit hash. OpenAI's own four-line patch note describes the whole bug: nobody checked what git actually checked out.

item.title: CagriSema vs. Tirzepatide: What the New Diabetes Trial Actually Shows
item.description: Novo Nordisk says its experimental drug CagriSema beat Eli Lilly's tirzepatide on weight loss in a head-to-head diabetes trial. It did — against a 5mg dose, not tirzepatide's strongest one. A second trial released the same day, against the 15mg dose, went the other way.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Is Cheaper and Faster — But the Real News Is What Anthropic Led With
item.description: On September 22, 2026, Anthropic shipped Claude Opus 5.5 — its first new model since CEO Dario Amodei published an essay ten days earlier arguing the whole industry should deliberately slow down. It's 40 percent cheaper than Opus 5, runs about 30 percent faster, performs close to the pricier Fable 5.1 — and the launch announcement opened with an alignment score, not a benchmark.

item.title: Why the Washington Supreme Court Struck Down I-2066
item.description: On September 17, 2026, a divided Washington Supreme Court ruled Initiative 2066 — the natural gas measure two million Washingtonians approved in 2024 — unconstitutional in its entirety. What the ruling actually says, what I-2066 actually did, what the dissent argued, and which justices from the ruling are actually on this November's ballot.

item.title: Fifty-Two Weeks, No Remainder
item.description: A study by Prof. Eshbal Ratzon of Tel Aviv University argues that the Qumran sect really did run its famous 364-day calendar in daily life — at least at first — and then quietly stopped, because 364 days is a day and a quarter short of a solar year and the error compounds. Here is what the calendar was for, why a number divisible by seven was worth that much trouble, what the roughly twenty calendrical scrolls actually contain, and why the argument matters to anyone reading Second Temple texts.

item.title: Nobody Wanted to Go First
item.description: When the UN's 81st General Assembly opens its general debate on September 22, Brazil's president speaks first, as every Brazilian president has, on and off, since the late 1940s. The standard one-line explanation — "a tradition dating to 1955" — is true, but it skips the six years in between when the honor actually changed hands three times.

item.title: The Calling Card in a Cat's Kidneys
item.description: Cat kidneys are stuffed with fat droplets, and nobody has known why for about 110 years. A study in Current Biology reports the answer: they are a reservoir for thirteen branched-chain fatty acids whose exact mix differs from cat to cat, holds steady within one animal, and survives on the ground for at least a day — a chemical calling card. Then the obvious follow-up, which has a real and complicated literature: do people have one too, and could you identify someone from it?

item.title: The Most-Downloaded AI Models in the World Are Alibaba's
item.description: On 18 September Alibaba's Qwen team shipped Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash — one model that takes text, images, audio and video, holds a million tokens of context, and decides for itself which parts of a two-hour video are worth watching. The release is the news, but the program behind it is the story: Qwen passed three billion downloads this summer, more than Google's and Meta's open models combined. Here is what "omnimodal" actually means, what the 26 percent is measuring, and why a company most people know for e-commerce is a serious AI lab.

item.title: 4.7 Sigma, and a New Kind of Spooky
item.description: CERN's ATLAS and CMS experiments have found strong evidence that pairs of Z bosons — the carriers of the weak nuclear force — come out of certain Higgs boson decays quantum entangled. It's the first time entanglement has been measured between two massive force-carrying particles rather than matter particles, and it happened because a Higgs boson has zero spin and a Z boson doesn't, which leaves the two Z bosons no honest way to be independent of each other. Here's what was actually measured, how sure they are, and what it isn't.

item.title: The Same Box, a Lot More Inside
item.description: Apple's new Mac Studio ships September 22 with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, up to 512GB of unified memory, and the same 7.7-inch-square case it's shipped since 2023. I've always liked Apple machines, and I was expecting a smaller redesign — it isn't one, and the real story turns out to be better than that: the same little box got a lot more machine crammed into it, at the same starting price.

item.title: Twice the Mass of Jupiter, and a Problem for How Stars Form
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope's newest, largest public image is a panorama of a stellar nursery called IC 348 — and buried in it are the smallest brown dwarfs ever confirmed, weighing in at about twice the mass of Jupiter. That number is smaller than the theory of how stars form says it should be able to produce, and one of the objects appears to have its own disk of material, meaning something that is itself barely planet-sized may be forming planets of its own.

item.title: The Mosquito That Can't Carry It
item.description: Malaria killed about 610,000 people in 2024, three quarters of them children under five. One approach to ending it does not spray anything, distribute anything, or ask anyone to take a pill — it edits the mosquito so the parasite cannot survive inside it, and lets the edit spread itself through the wild population. There are two schools of thought about how to do that, they disagree about whether the mosquito should live, and the better-funded one just had its field programme shut down by a government. This is how the mechanism works and where it actually stands.

item.title: The Summer of Truth, and the Things With Dates
item.description: Ursula von der Leyen's 2026 State of the Union names a war on the continent, a closed Strait of Hormuz that has cost Europe €90 billion, a €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China and a Russian drone attack in Leipzig — and the two proposals that leave the hall with a date attached are a Heatwave Plan and a ban on social media for children. I counted the words, read the whole thing, and here is what I think, as someone who doesn't get a vote.

item.title: The Same Barrel
item.description: Costco started rationing motor oil this week, a first in its history — two boxes of its own Kirkland Signature synthetic per member, per week. Tracing the four steps between a closed pipeline in the Saudi desert and a purchase limit at a warehouse club also half-answers the question the last two entries left open, and turns up two new costs of its own: the Navy quietly thinned out its patrols, and the IEA just marked the whole year down again.

item.title: What a Locked iPhone Still Gives Up
item.description: A phone-forensics demonstration circulating on X this week is a reminder that "only law enforcement has this" was never really the boundary — the tools, the vendors and the exploits all move. What a locked iPhone actually protects, what Advanced Data Protection does and doesn't cover, and a short history of who has had this capability and for how long.

item.title: Antarctica Gained 695 Billion Tons of Ice, and the Reason Was Seven Thousand Kilometres Away
item.description: Between July 2021 and April 2023 the Antarctic ice sheet got heavier by about 695 billion tons — the largest gain in the twenty-four-year satellite-gravity record. A paper in Nature traces it to a warm patch of tropical ocean that bent the atmosphere over East Antarctica and turned it into a snow funnel. The headline is a gift to anyone who wants to misread it. The paper is not: two decades of losses at 140 billion tons a year are still there, and the gain is a weather event, not a trend.
